quote: Gauss'sche Problem: Bestimmung der Verhältnisse der Häufig- keit der irregulären negativen Determinanten zur Häufig- keit der regulären.
english: Gauss's problem: determination of the ratio of the frequency of irregular negative determinants to the frequency of regular ones.
topic: Short notes on Gauss's problem about how often irregular and regular negative determinants occur, a claim that a continuous series-sum need not converge uniformly, a preference for Weierstrass's convergence method over Eisenstein–Kronecker's, and the start of a discussion of irrational numbers defined by fundamental sequences.

triage.modern_statement: In the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (around art. 306), Gauss calls a negative determinant D of binary quadratic forms ax²+2bxy+cy² 'regular' if the group of classes in its principal genus is cyclic, and 'irregular' if it is not. Under composition the principal genus is Cl(D)², the subgroup of squares in the form class group. The question asks what fraction of negative determinants (in modern terms, discriminants of imaginary quadratic orders or fields) are irregular as |D| goes to infinity, compared with the regular ones. Equivalently: as |D|→∞, how often is Cl(D)² non-cyclic? The odd part of Cl(D) sits inside Cl(D)², so the main piece is the question of how often the odd part of the class group is non-cyclic.
triage.answered_by: No one has proved it. It has a conjectured answer: the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics (H. Cohen and H. W. Lenstra Jr., 'Heuristics on class groups of number fields', Noordwijkerhout 1983, LNM 1068, published 1984). They predict that the odd part of the class group of an imaginary quadratic field is cyclic with probability about 97.757%, so 'irregularity' coming from odd primes should occur about 2.24% of the time. The 2-part (4-ranks) has been studied separately, e.g. by Gerth and by Fouvry–Klüners. Earlier computational work on Gauss's irregular determinants: D. Shanks (Math. Comp. 1969) and D. Buell (Math. Comp. 1976). This is not one of Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem.

evidence.claim: Gauss's terminology: a discriminant whose principal genus is non-cyclic is called irregular. Buell computed class groups of imaginary quadratic fields and found irregular examples.
Shanks's 1969 paper 'On Gauss's Class Number Problems' covers composition groups for negative determinants, including non-cyclic groups and irregular determinants.
Cohen–Lenstra note that the odd part of the class group of an imaginary quadratic field seems rarely non-cyclic. Their heuristic gives a probability of about 97.7% that the odd part is cyclic.
The Cohen–Lenstra prediction for the probability that the odd part of Cl_Δ (Δ<0) is cyclic is still being tested against large unconditional class group tabulations.
The Cohen–Lenstra principle grew into a large research area (Cohen–Martinet, Bhargava and others). A 2024 survey links it back to Gauss's quadratic forms.

triage.why: Hilbert's note restates Gauss's own question from the Disquisitiones about the density of irregular negative determinants, meaning those with a non-cyclic principal genus. The modern conjectured answer is the Cohen–Lenstra heuristics (1984), which predict about 2.24% non-cyclic odd parts. Only a few cases are proven (e.g. the Davenport–Heilbronn results on 3-torsion and Fouvry–Klüners on 4-ranks). The full density statement is still unproven, and Cohen–Lenstra-type questions are a very active field. I'm only at medium confidence because none of the sources I found states outright that Gauss's frequency question is the same as the Cohen–Lenstra cyclicity prediction. That link is my own reading, based on Gauss's definition and the papers cited. The exact density for Gauss's version (Cl², which includes the 2-part) was not checked.
